label: Data Movement Part 2: Pipelines and Connectors
topic: Data Movement: continuous data pipelines and connectors

questions.scenario: A Standard Edition account has a table with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1 and MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS left at its default. A stream on the table feeds a task. The task was suspended after repeated failures and nobody consumed the stream for 9 days. The stream holds unconsumed changes. An engineer now runs SHOW STREAMS and finds that STALE is FALSE.
questions.stem: Which statement explains this result and its cost?

options.text: The stream is not stale only because the retention of 1 day was reset each day by SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA calls on the stream.
Snowflake extended the table's retention to the stream's offset, up to MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS (default 14 days), and the extra retained history adds storage cost.
The extension applies only to Enterprise Edition or higher, so the Standard Edition stream must have been consumed by another process.
The stream is stale after 1 day, and SHOW STREAMS reports a stale stream as FALSE until the next query reads it.

explanation.correct: When a stream is not consumed, Snowflake extends the source table's data retention to the stream's offset, up to MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS, which defaults to 14 days. This applies regardless of edition and the extra retained history costs storage. Here 9 days is inside the 14-day window.

distractors.A: SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA prevents staleness only when the stream is empty and the function returns FALSE. This stream holds unconsumed changes, and nothing in the scenario calls the function.
distractors.C: The retention extension applies regardless of edition. Nothing needs to have consumed the stream.
distractors.D: SHOW STREAMS reports staleness directly through the STALE and STALE_AFTER columns. It doesn't wait for a query to mark a stream stale.

questions.scenario: A stream s_orders is defined on table orders and holds 100 unconsumed change rows. An engineer runs BEGIN; INSERT INTO audit_a SELECT * FROM s_orders; INSERT INTO audit_b SELECT * FROM s_orders; COMMIT;. After the transaction starts but before the first INSERT runs, another session inserts 20 new rows into orders and commits.
questions.stem: What happens when the transaction commits?

options.text: audit_a gets 100 rows and audit_b gets 0 rows, because the first INSERT moved the stream offset.
audit_a gets 100 rows and audit_b gets 120 rows, because tables and streams use read committed isolation.
audit_a and audit_b each get the same 100 rows, and the 20 new rows stay in the stream for the next consumption.
audit_a and audit_b each get 120 rows, because a stream is read as of the time each statement runs.

explanation.correct: Streams use repeatable read isolation. Within a transaction, every statement sees the stream as of the transaction start. The DML consumes the records only if the transaction commits, and changes committed by other transactions in the meantime appear after it.

distractors.A: The offset moves only when the transaction that uses the stream commits, not at the first INSERT. Both statements see the same records.
distractors.B: Tables use read committed isolation but streams use repeatable read. The two statements can't see different record sets.
distractors.D: A stream queried in an explicit transaction is read as of the transaction start, not the statement time, so the 20 later rows are excluded.

questions.scenario: A team wants a task that loads rows from the stream s_events into a target table only when the stream has data. They want no polling schedule and no compute spent until changes arrive. They also want Snowflake to manage the compute, so no warehouse is named.
questions.stem: Which task definition meets these requirements?

options.text: CREATE TASK t TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL = '15 MINUTES' WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;
CREATE TASK t WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;
CREATE TASK t WAREHOUSE = etl_wh WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;
CREATE TASK t SCHEDULE = '1 MINUTE' TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL = '15 MINUTES' WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;

explanation.correct: A triggered task has a WHEN clause on the stream and no SCHEDULE. A serverless triggered task omits WAREHOUSE and must set TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL.

distractors.B: A serverless triggered task requires TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL. Without it, and without a warehouse, the definition is incomplete.
distractors.C: Naming a warehouse makes this a user-managed triggered task. The requirement was for Snowflake-managed compute.
distractors.D: Adding SCHEDULE turns this into a scheduled task that checks the condition every minute and skips when empty. It is not event-triggered.

questions.scenario: A scheduled task graph has a root task and five child tasks. The fourth task in the chain fails at 02:10 after the first three have succeeded. The nightly run cannot wait for the next schedule. The team wants to rerun only the failed part of that run, without rerunning the tasks that already succeeded.

options.text: Run EXECUTE TASK on the root task with no extra clause.
Set TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 1 on the failed child task and wait.
Run EXECUTE TASK on the root task with RETRY LAST.
Run ALTER TASK on the failed child to RESUME it, which reruns it.

explanation.correct: EXECUTE TASK ... RETRY LAST reruns from the last failed task or tasks in the latest graph run, as a new run with the attempt number increased by one.

distractors.A: A plain EXECUTE TASK on the root starts a new full run of the graph, including the tasks that already succeeded.
distractors.B: TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS is set on the root, and when a child fails it retries the whole graph. It doesn't apply retroactively to the failed run.
distractors.D: RESUME changes the task's state and doesn't rerun it. The graph version is set when the root is resumed or executed.

questions.scenario: A data engineer owns several views and their underlying tables and has enabled change tracking on all of them. The engineer wants to create a stream on views that meet the requirements for streams on views.
questions.stem: Which TWO views can have a stream created on them? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A view that aggregates order totals per customer with GROUP BY
A view that returns SELECT DISTINCT customer_id from a table
A view that inner joins orders to customers and filters on region
A view defined over an external table
A view that combines two tables with UNION ALL

explanation.correct: A stream on a view allows projections, filters, inner or cross joins, and UNION ALL.

distractors.A: GROUP BY is not allowed in a view that has a stream.
distractors.B: DISTINCT is not allowed in a view that has a stream.
distractors.D: Views over external tables and directory tables are not supported for streams.

questions.scenario: A pipeline reads files that land in an S3 bucket through an external table. The team wants a stream on the external table to drive a downstream load. Files are sometimes removed from the bucket by a lifecycle rule, and those removals must not appear as deleted rows in the stream.
questions.stem: Which statement creates a stream that works for this external table?

options.text: CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t;
CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t APPEND_ONLY = TRUE;
CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = TRUE;
CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t INSERT_ONLY = TRUE;

explanation.correct: Streams on external tables must be insert-only. An insert-only stream records inserts only, so a file removed from cloud storage is not recorded as a delete.

distractors.A: A default stream is a standard stream, which also records deletes. External tables require INSERT_ONLY = TRUE.
distractors.B: APPEND_ONLY applies to standard tables, dynamic tables, Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables and views. External tables use INSERT_ONLY instead.
distractors.C: SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS only changes what the first consumption returns. It doesn't make the stream insert-only, so the stream type is still invalid for an external table.

questions.scenario: A table holds GPS pings in a GEOGRAPHY column. Rows are only ever inserted, and the table is truncated every night right after the load task consumes the new rows. A standard stream on this table does not return change data for the geospatial data. The team wants the cheapest stream that works.

options.text: A standard stream created with SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = TRUE
A stream created with APPEND_ONLY = TRUE
A stream created with INSERT_ONLY = TRUE
A standard stream created AT (OFFSET => -3600)

explanation.correct: Standard streams can't return change data for geospatial data, so an append-only stream is used. It records inserts only, is faster than a standard stream, and lets the source be truncated right after consumption without extra cost for the next query.

distractors.A: SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS affects only the first consumption. The stream is still a standard stream and still can't return geospatial change data.
distractors.C: INSERT_ONLY is for external tables and externally managed Iceberg tables, and for some Delta Direct tables. It is not the option for a standard table.
distractors.D: AT (OFFSET => ...) sets where the stream starts with Time Travel. It doesn't change the stream type.

questions.scenario: A deployment script runs CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders every release. The stream usually has unconsumed changes when the script runs. The team wants the replaced stream to keep the current offset, so that no pending changes are lost.

options.text: CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders AT (STREAM => 's_orders');
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders COPY GRANTS;
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = TRUE;
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders;

explanation.correct: AT (STREAM => 'name') starts the new stream at the same offset as the named stream. With OR REPLACE it keeps the current offset when the stream is recreated.

distractors.B: COPY GRANTS keeps the privileges, except OWNERSHIP. It doesn't carry over the offset.
distractors.C: SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS makes the first consumption return all rows that existed at creation, which would reprocess data that was already consumed.
distractors.D: A plain CREATE OR REPLACE starts a new stream at the current point. CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM is also a way to advance the offset without using the changes, so unconsumed changes are lost.

questions.scenario: The table sales is owned by role DATA_OWNER. Change tracking has never been enabled on it and no stream exists on it. Role ETL_ROLE has CREATE STREAM on the schema, USAGE on the database and schema, and SELECT on sales. When ETL_ROLE runs CREATE STREAM s_sales ON TABLE sales, the statement fails.

options.text: ETL_ROLE also needs OPERATE on the table before it can create a stream.
ETL_ROLE needs USAGE on a warehouse, because creating a stream starts the change tracking job.
Change tracking isn't enabled yet, and only the table owner can create the first stream on the table. DATA_OWNER can create it.
A stream can't be created on a table unless the creator role owns the schema.

explanation.correct: If change tracking isn't yet enabled on the table, only the table owner can create the first stream. Creating that stream enables change tracking.

distractors.A: OPERATE on a table is not a stream creation requirement. Creating a stream needs CREATE STREAM on the schema and SELECT on the source.
distractors.B: A warehouse is billed only when the stream is queried. The object itself has no charge, and a warehouse isn't a creation requirement.
distractors.D: The creator needs CREATE STREAM on the schema and some privilege on the database and schema, not ownership of the schema.

questions.scenario: A team is moving several tasks to serverless compute and reviewing how serverless sizing and the related parameters behave.
questions.stem: Which THREE statements about serverless tasks are correct? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Serverless sizing history is discarded on suspend, so a resumed task starts again from its initial size.
USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE defaults to MEDIUM and is ignored after a few successful runs.
USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE can be set together with WAREHOUSE to size the first run on that warehouse.
TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL has no effect once the task is already running at its maximum size.
Serverless tasks are the right choice for workloads larger than XXLARGE.
The maximum serverless size is XXLARGE, and SERVERLESS_TASK_MAX_STATEMENT_SIZE defaults to XXLARGE.

explanation.correct: The initial size parameter defaults to MEDIUM and stops mattering after a few successful runs. TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL is ignored once the task is at maximum size. The serverless maximum is XXLARGE, which is also the default of the max-size bound.

distractors.A: Serverless sizing history is kept across suspend and resume. It is removed only when the task is recreated with CREATE OR REPLACE.
distractors.C: Setting USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE together with WAREHOUSE is an error. The parameter applies only to serverless tasks.
distractors.E: Workloads larger than XXLARGE are a case for a user-managed warehouse, because serverless tops out at XXLARGE.

questions.scenario: A data engineer builds dt_silver with TARGET_LAG = '10 minutes' from a raw table. A second dynamic table, dt_gold, reads dt_silver. To avoid managing two lag values, the engineer creates dt_gold with TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM. Nothing else in the account reads dt_gold, because analysts query dt_silver directly.

options.text: The CREATE statement fails, because a DOWNSTREAM table must have at least one consumer.
dt_gold inherits the 10-minute lag of dt_silver and refreshes on that cadence.
dt_gold refreshes every 60 seconds, which is the minimum target lag.
dt_gold never refreshes automatically, and Snowflake gives no warning.

explanation.correct: A DOWNSTREAM table has no schedule of its own. It refreshes only when a downstream table needs it. With no consumer it never refreshes automatically, and Snowflake doesn't warn about it.

distractors.A: The statement succeeds. Snowflake doesn't validate that a DOWNSTREAM table has consumers.
distractors.B: DOWNSTREAM takes its lag from the consumers of the table, not from its upstream. It doesn't copy the upstream lag.
distractors.C: 60 seconds is the lowest value you can set for a target lag. It is not a default that DOWNSTREAM falls back to.

questions.scenario: A dynamic table was created with the default refresh mode. Its query used EXCEPT, so SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES reported refresh_mode = FULL with an unsupported-operator reason. The team has since rewritten the query without EXCEPT, and every construct is now supported incrementally. They want the table to refresh incrementally.

options.text: Recreate it with CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE and an explicit REFRESH_MODE such as ADAPTIVE.
Run ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE ... SET REFRESH_MODE = ADAPTIVE.
Suspend and resume the table so that AUTO is evaluated again.
Wait. AUTO re-evaluates the definition at every refresh and will switch.

explanation.correct: The refresh mode is set at creation and can't be changed with ALTER. AUTO is evaluated once at creation and the result is locked in. Use CREATE OR REPLACE (or CREATE OR ALTER, where some transitions reinitialize) with an explicit mode.

distractors.B: ALTER can't change the refresh mode.
distractors.C: Suspend and resume don't re-evaluate the mode. AUTO was resolved once at creation.
distractors.D: AUTO never switches after creation. The resolved mode is locked in.

questions.scenario: Three materialized views are defined on the table sales, and none of them reads the column discount_code. A developer drops discount_code from sales during a cleanup.
questions.stem: What is the effect, and what is the fix?

options.text: Nothing happens, because the views don't use the dropped column.
All materialized views on sales are suspended and can't be resumed. Recreate each with CREATE OR REPLACE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... COPY GRANTS.
The views are suspended, and ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW ... RESUME restores them once the table is stable.
The views are dropped automatically and must be created again, and their grants are lost.

explanation.correct: Changing or dropping a column on the base table suspends all materialized views on it, even if they don't use that column. They can't be resumed. Recreate them with CREATE OR REPLACE ... COPY GRANTS to keep the grants.

distractors.A: A changed or dropped column suspends every materialized view on the table, whether or not the view uses it.
distractors.C: RESUME doesn't work for this case, since these views can't be resumed.
distractors.D: The views are suspended, not dropped. COPY GRANTS on the recreate keeps the grants.

questions.scenario: Thousands of billing meters send readings to a service. Each meter's readings must land in the target table in order, with no duplicates after a client retry or restart. The business accepts latency of a few seconds. There are no files, and rows come straight from application code.

options.text: Snowpipe Streaming (high-performance) with Named Channels, one per source partition, resuming from the committed offset token
Snowpipe Streaming (high-performance) with Elastic Channels, where Snowflake manages one implicit channel per pipe
Snowpipe with auto-ingest, writing a file about once a minute to an external stage
The Snowpipe REST API, calling insertFiles for each reading

explanation.correct: Named Channels give exactly-once, ordered delivery within a channel using offset tokens, and the app can replay from the last committed offset. Rows arrive with latency of seconds and with no files.

distractors.B: Elastic Channels are at-least-once with no ordering, so a retry after an ambiguous failure can duplicate rows.
distractors.C: Auto-ingest works on files, with typical latency of about a minute, and doesn't track per-source ordering.
distractors.D: insertFiles queues staged files. It doesn't take rows and doesn't give per-source ordering.

questions.scenario: An application stages files and loads them through the Snowpipe REST API with a pipe created with AUTO_INGEST = FALSE. The team is writing the monitoring and permission model for it.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A 200 response from insertFiles means the files have been loaded.
insertReport returns load results for the last 14 days.
A file that failed, once corrected and resubmitted under the same path, loads again at once.
The pipe owner, not the calling user, needs the privileges on the stage and the table.
insertFiles accepts up to 5,000 staged files in one request.

explanation.correct: The pipe owner needs the load privileges (USAGE or READ on the stage, INSERT on the table). The caller needs OPERATE on the pipe for insertFiles. One insertFiles request can queue up to 5,000 staged files.

distractors.A: A 200 means the files are queued. Check insertReport, loadHistoryScan or COPY_HISTORY for the load result.
distractors.B: insertReport covers the last 10 minutes. loadHistoryScan covers a time range within the last 14 days.
distractors.C: Snowpipe remembers file paths for 14 days. Resubmitting a file under the same name doesn't reload it, even if it was corrected.

questions.scenario: A team writes a SQL UDF that formats a customer name and declares it RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT (STRICT), expecting Snowflake to skip the body and return NULL whenever the input is NULL. Some rows in the source table have NULL names, and the body calls a string function that fails on NULL.

options.text: The body is skipped for NULL inputs, so the string function never sees NULL.
STRICT isn't supported for SQL UDFs. They always run as CALLED ON NULL INPUT, so the body must handle NULLs itself.
The body is skipped only if the UDF is also declared IMMUTABLE.
Declaring the return type NOT NULL makes Snowflake reject NULL inputs before the body runs.

explanation.correct: STRICT (RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT) isn't supported for SQL UDFs. They are always called on NULL input, so the body has to handle NULLs, for example with COALESCE or IFNULL.

distractors.A: This is what STRICT does for other handler languages, but not for SQL UDFs.
distractors.C: IMMUTABLE is a promise about repeatable results and has no link to NULL handling. Snowflake doesn't check it.
distractors.D: NOT NULL isn't enforced for SQL UDFs.

questions.scenario: A custom application submits a long-running transformation with POST /api/v2/statements. The call returns HTTP 202 with a statement handle instead of a result set. The developer needs the application to get the final result without running the statement twice.

options.text: Treat the 202 as a failure and resubmit the same POST without a requestId.
Treat the 202 as a statement error, since statement errors return 202.
Cancel the statement with POST /api/v2/statements/{handle}/cancel and run it again.
Poll GET /api/v2/statements/{statementHandle} until the statement finishes, then read the result partitions.

explanation.correct: A 202 means the statement hasn't finished (or was submitted with async=true). Poll the statement handle with GET until it completes. The results come back in partitions that you can fetch with the partition parameter.

distractors.A: Resubmitting without a requestId can run the statement twice. A resubmission should carry the same UUID requestId and retry=true.
distractors.B: Statement errors return 422. A 202 means not finished.
distractors.C: Cancelling throws away the running work. The statement is still in progress, so there is nothing to retry.

questions.scenario: A company wants to replicate change data from an operational database and from several SaaS applications into Snowflake with Openflow. Security requires that the Openflow data plane runs inside the company's own cloud account, with Snowflake managing only the control plane.

options.text: BYOC (Bring Your Own Cloud)
Snowflake Deployments on Snowpark Container Services
Snowpipe Streaming with the Kafka connector v4
A Snowpipe pipe with AUTO_INGEST = TRUE

explanation.correct: BYOC runs the Openflow data plane in the customer's cloud, and Snowflake manages the control plane. Openflow is the Snowflake service for database CDC and SaaS sources.

distractors.B: Snowflake Deployments run on Snowpark Container Services in Snowflake, not in the customer's own cloud account.
distractors.C: This is a data ingestion path for Kafka topics and doesn't fit database CDC or SaaS sources. It isn't an Openflow deployment type.
distractors.D: Auto-ingest loads files that land in cloud storage. It isn't an Openflow deployment type and isn't meant for a database or SaaS source.

questions.scenario: An incremental dynamic table reads a base table with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS set to the default of 1. The dynamic table was suspended during a source migration and stayed suspended for three days. The engineer now tries to resume it.

options.text: The incremental refresh fails after resume, because change-tracking data expired. The only recovery is to drop and recreate the dynamic table.
RESUME works. The first refresh replays the three missed days of changes from the base table.
The first refresh fails, but raising the base table's retention to 7 days and running RESUME again recovers it.
Resume switches the table to FULL refresh mode for the first refresh, then returns to INCREMENTAL.

explanation.correct: If a dynamic table is suspended longer than the base tables' data retention period, the change-tracking data it needs expires. An incremental dynamic table then fails on resume, and the only recovery is to drop and recreate it.

distractors.B: The changes are no longer available after retention expires, so there is nothing to replay.
distractors.C: Raising retention doesn't bring back change data that has already expired. The notes give drop and recreate as the only recovery.
distractors.D: Resume doesn't change the refresh mode. The mode is fixed at creation.

questions.scenario: A team runs a chain of dynamic tables and plans to orchestrate some of them with an external scheduler. They are reviewing how suspension, the scheduler setting and cost work.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Suspending a dynamic table leaves its downstream dynamic tables refreshing on their own schedules.
Cloud Services cost for a dynamic table accrues only in refresh cycles where the base data changed.
After SCHEDULER = DISABLE, the table's TARGET_LAG is reported as NULL, and a manual refresh does not cascade to upstream or downstream dynamic tables.
SUSPEND is a permanent detach from scheduling that clears TARGET_LAG.
When an upstream table is resumed, a downstream table that a user suspended directly (USER_SUSPENDED) stays suspended.

explanation.correct: SCHEDULER = DISABLE detaches the table from scheduling: TARGET_LAG shows NULL and a manual refresh doesn't cascade, which suits external orchestrators such as dbt or Airflow. Resuming an upstream table also resumes downstream tables that were suspended by cascade, but not those a user suspended directly.

distractors.A: Suspending a dynamic table also suspends its downstream dynamic tables.
distractors.B: Cloud Services work (change detection, compilation, scheduling) runs on every refresh cycle, even when no data changed. Lengthening the lag cuts that cost.
distractors.D: SUSPEND is a temporary stop that keeps the configuration, including TARGET_LAG. The permanent detach is SCHEDULER = DISABLE.

questions.scenario: A team runs Kafka connector v4. To mask a column and cast another, they created a pipe with the same name as the destination table. They also set snowflake.validation=client_side so that bad records go to a dead-letter queue. At startup the connector task fails with ERROR_5030.

options.text: Set errors.tolerance=all, which lets the task continue past the error.
Rename the pipe to {tableName}-STREAMING so that the connector recognizes it.
Grant CREATE PIPE on the schema to the connector role.
Switch snowflake.validation to server_side, which is the default, or remove the user-created pipe.

explanation.correct: With client_side validation the connector works only in default pipe mode. A user-created pipe with client-side validation fails with ERROR_5030. A user-defined pipe needs server_side validation. The dead-letter queue then covers only converter errors, and invalid records go to the Error Table.

distractors.A: errors.tolerance controls how record errors are handled. It doesn't make a user-created pipe valid with client-side validation.
distractors.B: {tableName}-STREAMING is the name of the default pipe that the connector creates. A user-defined pipe takes the same name as the table.
distractors.C: CREATE PIPE is for the connector auto-creating a pipe in default pipe mode. The pipe here already exists, and the error is about the validation mode.

questions.scenario: A company runs Kafka connector v3 in the default Snowpipe ingestion mode and wants to move to v4 with no gaps or duplicates. The v3 connector is named orders-sink. Its committed offsets are stored in the Kafka consumer group connect-orders-sink.

options.text: Change connector.class on the existing orders-sink configuration to the v4 class and restart it.
Stop or delete the v3 connector, wait until the consumer group is Empty, then create the v4 connector with the same name. Keep snowflake.streaming.classic.offset.migration at skip.
Create the v4 connector under a new name so both run side by side until v4 catches up.
Create the v4 connector with the same name and set snowflake.streaming.classic.offset.migration to strict.

explanation.correct: v4 isn't a drop-in. The connector name decides the consumer group that holds the committed offsets, so keep the same name. Stop or delete v3 and wait until the group is Empty. Use the default skip setting for v3 Snowpipe mode, because it uses the Kafka consumer group offset.

distractors.A: v4 is a rewrite with a new connector class, different defaults and removed properties. Create a new configuration by hand.
distractors.C: A new name means a new consumer group, so the committed offsets are lost. Two connectors on the same topic also insert duplicates.
distractors.D: strict resumes from a v3 Snowpipe Streaming channel's committed offset and fails if the channel is missing. A Snowpipe-mode connector has no such channel, so use skip.

questions.scenario: A Spark job on a self-managed cluster writes a very large DataFrame to Snowflake. The transfer is expected to run for more than 36 hours. The team uses the default internal transfer, and earlier runs of this size failed partway through.

options.text: Keep internal transfer and set usestagingtable=off to avoid the temporary table.
Keep internal transfer and raise s3MaxFileSize so that fewer files are written.
Switch to external transfer with a bucket or container the team owns, and plan cleanup of its temporary files.
Set autopushdown to off, so that the work moves into Spark.

explanation.correct: Internal transfer uses temporary credentials that expire after 36 hours. For a transfer that is likely to take 36 hours or more, use external transfer with your own S3 or Azure bucket. Cleanup isn't automatic: set purge=on (Spark to Snowflake only), delete manually, or use a bucket lifecycle policy.

distractors.A: usestagingtable controls whether the load goes through a temporary table that is swapped in. It doesn't change the credential lifetime.
distractors.B: s3MaxFileSize is the file size for transfers from Snowflake to Spark. It doesn't change the credential lifetime.
distractors.D: autopushdown applies to reads that push Spark plans into Snowflake. It has no effect on a write's credential expiry.

questions.scenario: A Python job inserts 100,000 tuples with cursor.executemany() on a connection that uses paramstyle='qmark'. The connect() call sets user, account and authentication but not database or schema. The statement fails with an error about creating the temporary stage SYSTEM$BIND.

options.text: With server-side binding, large executemany inserts stream values through a temporary stage, so the session needs a current database and schema.
qmark placeholders are bound on the client, which can't send more than a few thousand rows at once.
executemany works only with pyformat placeholders, so qmark must be changed back.
executemany can't run an INSERT with bound values. The job should call execute_string instead.

explanation.correct: With server-side binding (qmark or numeric), executemany for an INSERT streams values above a threshold to a temporary stage. The session needs a current database and schema, or CREATE TEMPORARY STAGE SYSTEM$BIND fails.

distractors.B: qmark is bound on the server, not the client. The client-bound styles are pyformat and format.
distractors.C: executemany works with either binding style. Server binding is the better choice for batch inserts.
distractors.D: execute_string doesn't support bind parameters. executemany with server-side binding is the batch insert route.

questions.scenario: A company deploys the Snowflake native app connector for MySQL with its agent, which runs inside the company network. The team reviews the operating model before go-live.
questions.stem: Which THREE statements are correct? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Several agent instances should run in parallel against the same Native App instance for availability.
Tables without a primary key are not supported.
Replication mode is set per table, so each table can be continuous or scheduled.
The operational warehouse can be shared with other workloads to save credits.
In continuous mode the operational warehouse never suspends. To let it auto-suspend, switch all data sources to scheduled mode.
A table that failed permanently stays stopped until it is removed from replication and added again, which repeats the snapshot load.

explanation.correct: Tables need a primary key. The operational warehouse never suspends in continuous mode, so all data sources must be scheduled to allow auto-suspend. A permanently failed table is fixed by removing it from replication and adding it again, which repeats the snapshot.

distractors.A: Exactly one agent instance must run at all times. One agent connects to one Native App instance.
distractors.C: The mode is set per data source, not per table.
distractors.D: The operational warehouse can't be shared between instances or with other workloads. Only the compute warehouse may be shared.

questions.scenario: A v3 Kafka connector in Snowpipe mode loads a table. Checks show some rows duplicated, each with the same partition and offset in RECORD_METADATA. The Kafka Connect log shows CommitFailedException with the message that the group has already rebalanced. The loads take longer than the default 300,000 ms execution timeout.

options.text: Raise buffer.flush.time above its 120-second default.
Set behavior.on.null.values to IGNORE.
Raise consumer.max.poll.interval.ms to 900000, or lower consumer.max.poll.records to 50, in the Kafka Connect worker configuration.
Raise tasks.max above the number of CPU cores.

explanation.correct: Duplicates with the same partition and offset come from a load that exceeds the default 300-second execution timeout, which triggers a rebalance and a retry. Raise consumer.max.poll.interval.ms to 900000 or lower consumer.max.poll.records to 50.

distractors.A: buffer.flush.time controls when buffered records are written to a file. A longer value doesn't shorten the poll cycle.
distractors.B: behavior.on.null.values controls how NULL records are handled. It has no link to rebalance retries.
distractors.D: More tasks raise memory use and rebalances. Snowflake recommends the total number of partitions, not more than the CPU core count.

questions.scenario: A nightly Spark job refreshes a Snowflake table with SaveMode.Overwrite. The table has a GEOGRAPHY column, but after each run the column is VARCHAR, because the Spark column is a StringType holding WKT text. The team wants to keep the table's schema, including GEOGRAPHY.

options.text: Set continue_on_error=on.
Set usestagingtable=off.
Set column_mapping=name.
Keep the existing table with GEOGRAPHY and write with truncate_table=on.

explanation.correct: SaveMode.Overwrite replaces the table and its schema, so a StringType column becomes VARCHAR. With truncate_table=on, the connector truncates the table and keeps its schema. Write to an existing table that already has the GEOGRAPHY column.

distractors.A: continue_on_error=on skips bad rows. It doesn't affect the schema.
distractors.B: usestagingtable=off loads directly instead of into a temporary table that is swapped in. The overwrite still replaces the schema.
distractors.C: column_mapping=name changes how columns are matched. It doesn't stop an overwrite from replacing the table.

questions.scenario: A Python job runs a query that returns a very large result and wants several worker processes to download different parts of the result at the same time, instead of one process fetching all rows.

options.text: cursor.get_result_batches(), then hand different ResultBatch objects to different workers.
cursor.fetch_pandas_all() in every worker.
cursor.fetchmany() repeatedly in a single loop.
cursor.execute_async(), which returns results from parallel threads in order.

explanation.correct: get_result_batches() returns ResultBatch objects. Each has rowcount, sizes, and to_arrow() and to_pandas(), so you can send different batches to different workers to fetch in parallel. It returns None if the query hasn't finished.

distractors.B: fetch_pandas_all() pulls the whole result into one DataFrame in one process.
distractors.C: fetchmany() in a loop is a sequential fetch in one process.
distractors.D: execute_async() submits a query without waiting. It doesn't parallelize fetching, and async queries don't guarantee ordered results.
